utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. May the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-98-29/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is Mr. Milosevic in court? Mr. Milosevic, can you understand and follow the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you and I understand you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may remain seated, even when you're speaking. Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, David Akerson on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'm here with Manoj Sachdeva, trial attorney, and Biljana Blazevic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Appearances for Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. My name is Branislav Tapuskovic and I represent Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. I'm assisted by the lawyer Branislava Isailovic, who is a lawyer from Paris. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. Pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Trial Chamber or the Trial Judge has to convene a Status Conference within 120 days of the initial appearance of the accused in order to organise exchanges between the parties as to the -- and to ensure expeditious preparation for trial and to review the status of the accused's case and to allow the accused the opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including his mental and physical condition. I hope everybody has a copy of the agenda before them. Do you have it, Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do not?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Tapuskovic? Okay. Maybe then I'll just keep calling the items as we go along and we'll deal with them as we go along. Are there any outstanding motions? I'm made to understand that there is a motion filed by -- on behalf of the accused for provisional release. Obviously, I don't know when this was filed. I only heard of it this morning. I would imagine that the Prosecution still has to respond to if even before a decision can be made on it. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have a written response that will be filed very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And that's the only outstanding motion. Thank you very much. Now, at the last Status Conference on the 28th of March 2006, the Prosecution declared that 424 exhibits were awaiting translation. What is the position at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: If I'm understanding that item correctly, Your Honour, these are English exhibits that are to be translated into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Into Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes. We've had a number of conversations with Defence counsel regarding these exhibits and we have asked that the Defence counsel actually make the request themselves in order to get those translated for a couple of reasons. One, according to the Rules we are not obligated to translate English exhibits into Croatian so we are not doing it for the Office of the Prosecutor and we already have many requests for translations that we do -- we are required to make. Also, we are not doing this for the Court because this is -- they are already in English so they are already in a language that you can understand. These documents need to be translated, if at all, for Defence counsel. So we have met with them, we've discussed it in a number of -- two meetings specifically, and I believe they've agreed to -- just to make the request themselves so they can advance it because they can then prioritise the request themselves because we don't know which of these documents are most important that they need to prioritise. That being said, Your Honour, any assistance we can provide to Defence counsel, we are happy to do that. But we would prefer for these documents, since we really have no vested interest in them, that the Defence counsel assume responsibility for these and make the request themselves. So that's the status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Akerson. Mr. Tapuskovic? Do you confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very glad you have raised this issue at the Pre-Trial Conference. This is a very serious issue for us at this point in time, and it is making it impossible for the Defence to adequately prepare for trial. The accused must have access to documents that he can understand so that he can make certain suggestions to us on the basis of these documents. At the previous Pre-Trial Conference the Prosecution undertook the obligation to provide those documents in translation. But given the trials that were in course at the time they didn't -- it wasn't possible to deal with this issue. The Prosecution undertook this obligation. But without these documents we can't prepare for trial in an adequate way. At that point in time I mentioned two very illustrative examples, witnesses 56 and 124. These are witnesses that will be called by the Prosecutor and I'm familiar with these cases. I know that all the documents on those -- about those witnesses were translated in the case of Slobodan Milosevic. So I still can't understand why those two witnesses, who are extremely important for the Defence -- well, we haven't obtained any of the documents in translation. Given the resources we have, it's impossible for us to deal with things. We can only see our accused a couple of times a month. It's impossible for us to work on various issues if we don't have translations. These are documents in which one word is of crucial importance; everything depends on one word. So my colleague and myself understand French above all, so, on the basis of Rule 21, item 1(A), it's the Prosecution's obligation to enable us to obtain the material that we need by the service that is competent at this. We will request our evidence to be translated when the time comes, to present that evidence. In spite of all our efforts, we are very handicapped when it comes to preparing our defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, as I understood the Prosecutor's position is that the documents are there for the asking. All you need to do is to ask because they are not able to know what it is out of the 424 that you would need and they would like you to make a request. And as soon as you make the request, they will provide you with the documents. Or with the translation, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: If I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think that's precisely the question, Your Honour, is that Defence counsel have equal access to submit these documents for translations themselves. We are happy to facilitate this, if the Court -- if you would like us to, we can submit them. But it's awkward because we are not doing it for us, we are doing it for Defence counsel. And it seems to make more sense that they just assume responsibility and submit them themselves. But that being said we want to get these done and out of the way so that we can all proceed to trial. So whatever Your Honour prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe it might be -- okay, you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are two problems. With regard to the 424 documents, they've already requested their translation and we were expecting this to be done by -- in two months' time but I don't understand why we are not being provided with the documents that have already been translated in the case of those two witnesses that I mentioned, as an example. I don't understand why this material wasn't immediately provided to us, why the translated material wasn't provided to us because the Prosecution had such material. In the case of Slobodan Milosevic these witnesses have already been examined and all this material has already been translated so I don't understand why the Prosecution cannot provide us with documents that have already been translated, documents that refer to very important evidence. The Prosecution has already requested that the 424 documents be translated. But then there is the other issue why: Don't we have the material that has already been translated? We haven't received translated statements, translated evidence and I know this has been translated. It's not necessary to request that material that has already been translated be translated again. That would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Two issues are raised here, Mr. Akerson. Anything on the two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that any translation that we have, we provide to the Defence counsel. No questions asked. If he wants to alert us specifically to these two witnesses, we can check and see if there is translations but every translation that I know of that's in our possession we provide of course to Defence counsel. It is only the matter of these other documents that need to be translated who is going to be responsible for that, but as to these specific witnesses I can meet with Defence counsel after the fact and see if we have them. I'm not aware that we have any translations that have not been disclosed but I'll be happy to check again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you would do that. Maybe if we could just make an order that the Prosecution will check, at least the specifically for the two witnesses, witness statements, and if you find any translated statements of those two witnesses, provide them to the Defence. And also assist the Defence to get translations of the 424 documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Would you like us to make the requests ourselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could. It looks like it will expedite things if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's fine. We will be happy to do that. And I just would assure the Court that any translation we get at any time, we always would give that to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would that be okay? That will dispose of the matter that way, then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. On the question of disclosures, Rule 66(A)(i) disclosures, at the Status Conference held on the 12th of October 2005, the Prosecution submitted that disclosure under this rule had been completed which was contested by the Defence. Have the parties resolved this difference in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: To my knowledge, 66(A)(i) is complete, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had a couple of meetings and at those meetings we managed to find the necessary solutions, adequate solutions. I don't want to tie you with any other issues here. We've had a -- we've prepared a letter that we'll provide the Prosecution with. This concerns some of the issue that is you have raised. With regard of four of the statements that we have received, I can say that we still haven't received the translations of those statements into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which statements are these now, Mr. Tapuskovic? I thought we talked about them --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the letter that we have written for the Prosecution, we mentioned these statements. I can mention these statements now, if you like. Witness 98, 46, 125, Witness 61, and there are two statements that we received with supporting material and I wouldn't like to mention the names. This is confidential. So there are six statements in total, the translations of which we have not received. And there are some documents that the Prosecution states that they have provided us with but we've managed to file or register all those documents to examine them but there is significant number of documents that we haven't received. We have a list which we'll provide the Prosecution with after this conference and then I'll see which documents are concerned. Out of 22 witnesses who were UN representatives and protective measures were requested for them, only six of those witnesses have been identified and 16 of them haven't yet been identified. Your Honour, perhaps these statements were provided to us a long time ago. We know about 60 witnesses or so but witnesses or 16 witnesses who have been put forward and we still don't know what their identity is. We still haven't received expert reports. We haven't got reports of the experts who will be working for the Prosecution. This is very important for the Defence so that we can prepare an adequate Defence. And finally, I hope that these issues we will be able to resolve in discussions with the Prosecution. We have a motion that we will provide them with that there are these four or five items that in a certain sense hadn't been dealt with, haven't been disclosed, and as a result the Defence cannot examine such material. I think that's all I have to say for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. This problem seems to be sort of running through from one Status Conference to another. At the last Status Conference the Prosecution indicated that this was complete, this disclosure was complete. The Defence disputed that again. You are still disputing it today. May I suggest, Mr. Tapuskovic, that you meet with the Prosecution after this and sort out everything, just give the Prosecution every document that you say you do not have, which you are entitled to, which I should have had under Rule 66(A)(i), let it know what it is that's outstanding and hopefully they will provide the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was precisely our wish and we have it all in writing so that the Prosecution can see exactly what it is that I was talking to you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then can we resolve it on that basis then and hopefully we can get it off the item of the next Status Conference. Okay. Thank you very much. The next disclosure issue was in terms of Rule 66(A)(ii), and then in terms of this one, at the Status Conference of the 28th of March this year, the Defence submitted that they had not received the statements of eight victims whom the Prosecution intends to call. What is the position? Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said a while ago these are mainly not victims. As for the statements of victims we have mainly received those. This is some sort of a misunderstanding. These are witnesses who are supposed to speak about the problems which existed at the time so they are not victims. That is the number of witnesses which I indicated a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much, then. Then that can also be resolved similarly as the problems under 66(A)(i). Would that be okay with you, Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any issues that the parties would like to raise in terms of Rule 68? Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Regarding Rule 68, we've met with Defence counsel. He has provided us with a list of topics that he would like us to search for in our collections. We've done that. That's ongoing. Hopefully, by the end of next week, we can provide them with the bulk of the results of those searches. There are some documents that need to be cleared under Rule 70 still and there are some documents that are witness statements and we need to search other cases to make sure witness protections aren't in place but we will try to do that as quickly as possible. But hopefully the bulk of that disclosure will be done by the end of not this week but the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would just like to say about one thing that was mentioned by Mr. Tapuskovic, there are UN witnesses that are on the 65 ter list that are referenced as UN witness. They were all protected under Rule 7340. We have pending requests to get those cleared. We've received six of them so far and of course as soon as we get the clearance on the others we will provide those names. But the attending statements with them have already been provided, so it's only the -- literally the name that remains outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But all those things are being attended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. Do you have any comments to make on that, Mr. Tapuskovic? Or are you happy with what the Prosecution said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regrettably, Your Honour, I do have an objection which -- with reference to Rule 68. It is true the Prosecution has submitted to us a number of statements relevant to that issue but I have to quote 68, the brief, "the Prosecutor shall disclose to the Defence any material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused," and I'm quite sure that the Prosecutor already has knowledge that these -- this is evidence that can be used under Rule 68. However, everything which has been submitted to us by the Prosecution so far has been submitted in a way which states that they are being submitted both under Rule 68 and under Rule 66, so that this is an enormous quantity of material. Namely, the Prosecution has never submitted to us one single bit of evidence decidedly saying that according to their knowledge it is in the spirit of Rule 68. It is very confusing for us. It is so voluminous, it is such a huge quantity of material, and such a bulk of evidence. So can I ask the Prosecution when they do submit to us something under Rule 68 which they are definitely sure of, that they should spell out that it is under Rule 68. Not 68/66, because it is really hard for us then to handle such material and that is a problem for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any comment, Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think that the simple response, Your Honour, is that under Rule 66 we have an obligation to provide that document in a language to the accused. So it's in their advantage that we designate them as both Rule 66 and 68, which they often are. I mean, we designate them according to the rules that we think they apply to. But if we only designate them as Rule 66 -- or 68, I'm sorry, there isn't an obligation to translate it. And so I think it's to their advantage to actually have them designated properly by both rules, if they apply, because then we submit them for translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, but I guess the point that Mr. Tapuskovic is making is that if material is designated Rule 66/68, then they are not sure which of that material is specifically Rule 68 material. Of course, the problem can be solved by them reading the documentation and that's sort of asking you to do the reading for them and sorting it out for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that if any document, if we disclose it and we think it has some Rule 68 exculpatory value, we designate it as such. It may also be being disclosed under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- so we flag it with both rules. But that means it's Rule 68 in some respect, and I think we are obligated to do that, to designate both rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic, if material is disclosed to you, surely the idea is for you to read through that material and you see the Prosecution says that some material does come under both rules, both 66 and 68, and that's why they then put it 66/68 because it applies under both rules. It is anticipated that you're going to read that and whatever is exculpatory in that material then you would regard it as 68 material, and you would then use it at trial for that purpose. And whatever is 66 material you will use it for that purpose. Is it not -- isn't that what is -- what the case should be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand full well what you're saying and that is only logical, of course, but Rule 68 is a very specific one. I am talking about when the Prosecutor has ascertained that some material is indeed exculpatory and knows that for a fact, so everything that has been submitted to us so far, absolutely, and this refers to everything, it has never been specifically indicated it goes under Rule 68. I simply don't see -- I'm quite sure that the Prosecution knows nor a fact what evidently falls under 68 specifically, it can be five or ten materials, I do not insist on the exact number but to indicate every time that it comes under either 66 or 68 is something which leads us into an absurd situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like you're going to have again to talk to your learned friend on the opposite side on this issue because what I understand him to be saying is that simply some material falls under both rules and that is why they flag it as 66/68 material. And he also says that when they flag it as 66, then that's to your advantage because then they are responsible for the translation. But if it is only 68 then you've got to sort out your own translation. Maybe it may be helpful if you can sit down, as you do with the other items that we have been talking -- that we've talked, to sit down with your opposite number and sort out your difficulties. It's going to be very difficult to sort them out here in court. I can say read the material and check out which is 68 and which is 66. I could say this must be done by the Prosecution but does it really solve the problem? If you sit together and sort these things out I think it will be much easier that way. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course it is -- would be only normal that the two sides would have to sit down and agree on all these matters. I don't mind being submitted a document in English. I will have it translated at my own expense, but I cannot believe that in this case there hasn't been a single document in respect of which they could have said immediately and decidedly that it was a document of such character, even if it be just one or a couple, ten documents. But the fact that not a single piece of material has been flagged as under Rule 68, even if it is in English, that is something which I find hard to believe. If I have to go through -- weigh, every piece of evidence which I get from the Prosecution to see which one falls under which category, then I think that complicates matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are standing up, Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: And I guess it's important to note that if -- and I think this may be one source of confusion which I'll be happy to meet with Defence counsel and discuss further, but if we identify something as Rule 66/68, it is because they are both things not because it's one or the other and I guess that may be a point of clarity. I'm also looking at our disclosure list and there are a number of things that we have disclosed that are designated as only 68. There's a number of things that are designated as Rule 66. And there are some that are designated as both. So we have disclosed under all rules -- in both -- under both rules, individually and together. I guess it's also important to note that we are talking -- I think we've used 66(A) and 66(B), and I think what Defence counsel is referring to is 66(B). And just to be clear on that particular point, we are not obligated to disclose under 66(B). Under 66(A), of course, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe, as I say, from what you are saying, it's quite clear that only a meeting of the two groups will sort this -- these things out, because now you're saying to me that there is material that is disclosed that is under 68 only and he's saying not a single document has been identified as 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So I think if you could sit down and sort these things out.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So it's ordered. Are there any other matters that -- before we go to any other matters, let me raise the issue about the state of health of the accused. Mr. Tapuskovic, anything that you would like to tell us about the accused's state of health, either physically or mentally?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that perhaps it is best if that question was put to him but as far as I know he is in excellent state of health both physically and mentally, and as far as I know he has not had any objections in respect of the treatment being accorded him in the Detention Unit or in respect of his health condition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay then we'll go straight to the accused himself. Mr. Milosevic, do you have any complaints regarding your state of health or -- both physically or mentally or the conditions at the UNDU?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I'm very pleased indeed to be asked questions of this kind which attests to the kind of attitude being accorded to people in my situation. To your question, I should like to respond that I have no objections whatsoever to the work of the staff in the Detention Unit, nor do I have any objections generally speaking in respect of my conditions. As regards my health condition, as they say, thank God it is good. Perhaps sometimes it won't do for one to boast of one's good health condition but it is good, both physically, mentally and in every other respect. I don't have any problems either with respect to communication with my family or any -- or in any other respect. If you will allow me, I would have a couple of other comments to make in this particular regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me today for the first time at this Status Conference that there has been some headway made along the lines the Prosecution, the Defence, namely that after a lot of time has elapsed, there has been some sort of a rapprochement of their positions. With that, I should like to express the hope that what Mr. Tapuskovic has raised will be indeed resolved so that I would be able to find my bearings in this entire situation more easily and to also give my input to the Defence, preparation of the Defence, because the previous Status Conferences, in my view, evolved a bit differently. There was not as true, true insight into the actual situation and the problems attending it. I of course appreciate the positions of both parties, also in view of the voluminosity of the materials involved. I do hope that we can perhaps reduce the material to the substantive issues, including to what I said the last time. I don't have to have access to materials which refer to the Serbian Krajina, et cetera, which have nothing to do with me. So I should like to stress that as a contribution from my part, so as to expedite matters. Having said all this, Your Honour, I should also like to add that I've been here for 19 months now and the question was initiated twice of my conditional release pending the actual trial so far, but this was refused. This provisional release was refused, but I wish to say that by my general attitude and position, I actually have shown that it is possible for me to be outside the Detention Unit pending the actual trial so I would like to appeal on you -- to you that that be done if at all possible. If not, then I really have nothing to add. I should like to thank you, Your Honour, everything is all right, everything is okay, I really have nothing to add to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milosevic. The Chamber does appreciate your comments, and I thank you very much for your candid expression of your views. And I'm also happy to hear that you are in very good health. I think it's a very good point to make note of. I am sympathetic to the fact that you have been in detention for 19 months. But you know these trials take time, and everything possible will be done and I'm sure has been done also before to try to get your case to trial, and I can assure you that everybody in court here is working very hard to get your case to trial as soon as possible. Regarding your application for conditional release, you will remember that at the beginning of this conference this afternoon, we started about that point. I did acknowledge that we have received your new application. The Prosecution must get an opportunity to respond to that, and then the Court will make its decision. So I'm not able to give you a decision on that point right now and I'm sorry if that disappoints you, but that's how the process works. Okay? So your application will be considered and you'll hear in due course. Thank you very much. You may be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any other issues that the parties would like to raise which perhaps the Court may have missed? Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Only one small issue, Your Honour, that is that on May 10th of this year we filed a proposal to the Defence which was a list of facts for potential agreement, 40 pages of facts, and they range from things that are likely to be at issue at trial to things that are likely not to be at issue at trial. And we've had a meeting with both Defence counsel individually and discussed this motion. It seems that we are not advancing on this and I would just suggest that the Court contemplate that maybe being more proactive in getting involved in this issue, because I think there's a number of facts that we could probably agree on but it may take maybe another Pre-Trial Conference dedicated or status -- Pre-Trial Conference dedicated to this issue, to maybe try to push the parties to come to agreement on some of the more mundane issues that aren't going to be in agreement. I know that's not kind of the normal course of things here, but I think a little more proactive effort might actually be able to save some trial time in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic? Any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, naturally we've worked on these issues with the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. We've dealt with these issues. I must admit, and this is very important in this case, I must admit the following. You know that the Accused Galic was put on trial, that his trial concerned a different period of time with regard to the period of time that concerns Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. And since his trial has been -- or this case has been going for a while we thought we would have the judgement, the valid judgement from that case. That would provide us with certain guidelines and this has provided us with a -- or caused us a certain problem because we cannot examine facts that are undisputed. As far as I know but I'm not sure, I think that there are very few facts that were considered to be undisputable. With regard to facts that are well known, that don't have to be dealt with, with regard to the facts that can facilitate the work of the court, it's also in our interest not to deal with matters that are not in dispute. That we need an adequate analysis of such material, material the Prosecution has amounts to 40 pages, but for the moment I really can't tell you when we could provide you with a precise answer. We only have a few days to go and see the accused and speak to him. That's what the Registry allows us. As soon as we are in a position to provide you with more precise information about this matter, about reaching an agreement, on facts that are not in dispute, well, as soon as it's possible we will inform you of our agreement. But you should bear in mind everything that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic, but what I don't understand in what you are saying is how your agreement on whether or not the documents that have been submitted to you are agreed facts or not, how that is dependent on the judgement in the Galic matter. I don't think, if the Galic matter does come to finality and we get the judgement, so be it, but I don't think we can wait until that judgement is -- comes out before we resolve what is common cause between the parties. I would imagine that the parties should be able to identify issues that are common cause. I understand that you say you see the accused for very short periods of time on three occasions. I cannot understand why that is so if you're supposed to prepare for his trial. How often actually do you see the accused for professional work, I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, if we could see him more frequently we could do so but the registry has its principles that it adheres to, and as a result we can see the accused twice a month for two days on each occasion. And that's not sufficient time for us to be able to reach agreement with him. There are certainly facts that we will consider to be indisputable, especially with regard to certain general issues but at this point in time, we can't respond to that very voluminous motion made by the Prosecution. We will attempt to do so before the trial commences but at the moment, we really are not in a position to respond so rapidly to the Prosecution's suggestion as to the facts that could be considered to be indisputable. We'll do our best, of course, to do whatever we can, to do whatever is possible, but at this point in time, we cannot establish what our general position is with regard to all those facts that the Prosecution believes are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give an estimate of time when you think you may have got your instructions and be able to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this depends on when we will receive the material that we have to be provided with. The important documents that -- I don't know when the trial might start. We haven't mentioned this, we haven't discussed this issue today; but it would be very good if we had a vague idea. This is very important, as to when the trial might commence. Does anyone have at least a vague idea of when the trial might commence? I don't know how I can respond to the Prosecution's suggestion at the moment since I don't even know when the trial might commence but I'll do my best to act expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I also don't know when the trial might commence but the sooner these -- these issues are resolved, the sooner will the trial commence. It doesn't help to say, "Tell me when the trial will commence so that I can then expedite things." You've got to expedite things so that we can know when we can schedule the trial date. So I'm asking you to not hang what you are going -- what you have to do on when you are going -- when the trial is going to start but rather to do what you have to do so that we can see that the case is ready for trial. The case will get to trial when it is ready for trial and we've got to get it ready for trial, and getting it ready for trial includes, amongst other things, your agreeing with your opposite number on what may be agreed facts between the two of -- between the parties. And I understand that you say you've got very limited time for consultation with your client but within what is allowable, I'm asking to you please give priority to looking at those agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is misunderstanding, that's quite obvious. What you have said is correct but we will certainly act in this way before we file a pre-trial brief. There are a lot of facts that could be agreed on but we have to analyse everything very carefully. We are attempting to analyse the documents provided to us by the Prosecution very carefully. We are trying to gather our own evidence, and only once we have examined all of this material will it be possible for us to express our position with regard to the facts that are not in dispute. We will do our best to deal with all these issues and to reach agreement with the Prosecution as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say. I go back to my earlier question. Are you able to give an estimate of time when you think you can revert to your -- to the Prosecution on the agreed facts, proposed agreed facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do our best to discuss this issue whenever we meet the Prosecution. On all such occasions we will deal with this issue and try to define our respective positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. We -- I suppose we will have to leave that point on the basis that you will also sort it out with the Prosecution like you do the rest of the other issues. Anything else, Mr. Akerson, on your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any issue that you would like to raise, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, that will conclude the conference. And the Court now stands adjourned. Court adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
